title: Establishing phased assemblies and fine mapping of complex genomic regions encoding NK cell receptors and their implication in skin disease
text:
Variation in genes encoding natural killer (NK) cell receptors has been strongly implicated in susceptibility to viral
infections, cancers, and autoimmune disorders, including pemphigus, a life-threatening blistering disease
affecting thousands of Americans. In this project, we propose a comprehensive characterization of both
sequence and structural variation across genomic regions encoding NK cell receptors. This work will generate
the most complete map to date of these unusually complex genomic regions and will provide critical insights into
how variation within these regions contributes to pemphigus susceptibility.

title: Erm(41) Mediated Macrolide Resistance in Mycobacterium abscessus
text:
Mycobacterium abscessus is an emerging human pathogen that causes serious and difficult-to-treat infections.
The erm(41) gene confers resistance to macrolide antibiotics in M. abscessus, creating a significant hurdle to
effective treatment. The proposed research will investigate molecular mechanisms of Erm(41) function and may
lead to improved clinical diagnostics and treatment strategies by elucidating previously unknown aspects of
Erm(41)-mediated macrolide resistance.

title: Statistical Methods for Multilevel Multivariate Functional Studies
text:
Project narrative.
The project provides statistical analysis methods for quantiﬁcation of the evolution in the intensity of
brain lesions on multi-sequence Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Methods are motivated by the
need to develop new neuroimaging-based biomarkers for multiple sclerosis (MS), but can be applied
to other types of brain diseases including stroke, Alzheimer disease, and cancer.

title: Fundamental underpinnings of adult subtype diversification in spinal motor neurons
text:
Many neurodegenerative diseases like Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis and Huntington’s cause
neurodegeneration specifically during adulthood, and in specific kinds of neurons, suggesting that both age
and identity of a neuron are important for disease vulnerability. In this work we will study how embryonic motor
neurons mature into distinct subtypes of adult motor neurons, which are essential for controlling voluntary and
involuntary body movement, and are differentially affected in diseases. We will map the molecular properties of
adult motor neuron subtypes and determine which of these properties are required for normal function with the
goal of using this information to develop better treatments for diseases like Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis and
spinal cord injury.

title: Core B. Genomics and Bioinformatics Core
text: SUMMARY- CORE B (GENOMICS CORE) Core B (Genomics Core) will provide key support to the mVACS team in Clostridioides difficile genome sequence analysis, antigen design, microbiome sequence analysis, routine statistical analysis, and high content data management. Core B will use advanced genomics-based methods to quantify C. difficile genome composition and genetic variation, and associate these with outcomes. Core B will support analysis of protein structure to allow expression of well-folded domains as mRNAs. Core B will characterize DNA inversion systems and other mechanisms of DNA modification and alterations in gene activity that may impact vaccine efficacy. Core B will also carry out transcriptional profiling on C. difficile isolated from the intestine of vaccinated and immunodeficient mice, to assess how C. difficile responds in vivo to effective and ineffective immune responses. The Aims of Core B are: (1) C. difficile genomics to identify optimal targets for modified mRNA vaccines. Long read and short read data will be merged to generate complete assemblies, as in our previous work. Gene content will be enumerated and compared with clinical outcomes. (2) To assess variation in sequence and abundance of C. difficile vaccine targets. C. difficile isolates are known to encode considerable variation in their surface proteins. In addition, DNA inversion systems encode on-off switches affecting surface proteins and transcription factors, resulting in extensive population heterogeneity. This Aim will thus carry out deep assessment of proteins relevant as modified mRNA vaccine targets, and guide antigen design. (3) Transcriptional profiling and microbiome sequencing for mechanistic investigation. Projects 1-3 and the Clinical Core will generate murine and human fecal samples associated with successful or unsuccessful responses to C. difficile infection; Core B will quantify microbiome composition and metatranscriptomic analysis of C. difficile positive samples by RNA-seq. This core will oversee sequence acquisition and analysis is support of these studies. (4) Data management and archiving. Core C will work with Core A for standard statistical analysis and will archive and manage the diverse data types generated by the U19 team.

title: Proteostasis and Phosphate Sensing in the Regulation of the Phosphate Transporter SLC20A1
text:
While phosphate is involved in many fundamental cell processes including DNA synthesis, bone formation, and
storage of energy in high energy phosphates, it is unknown how mammalian cells sense and regulate phosphate
homeostasis to avoid deficiency or excess. Phosphate deficiency can lead to serious complications including
muscle breakdown; conversely, phosphate excess predisposes to heart attacks and strokes, which is especially
problematic for many of the 60% of Americans who are affected by chronic kidney disease over their lifetime.
Our preliminary work has identified several pathways that regulate cellular phosphate homeostasis and sensing
of phosphate availability that are the foundation of this proposal.

title: Ultrafast optical brain imaging via blurred matrix completion
text:
The brain is a complex organ consisting of many cell types that interact through many distinct
biochemical interactions. Linking molecular-level dynamics to brain-wide information flow requires the
ability to interrogate these many local signals, which often fluctuate on timescales as fast as
milliseconds, over large areas of the brain. Optical imaging of fluorescent tags has emerged as a key
technique in this endeavor, with brighter and faster optical sensors being increasingly improved and
expanded to tag biological targets of interest from calcium and voltage to glutamate, dopamine and
others. To match these improvements, and anticipate the constant trajectory of future indicators, the
next generation of optical microscopy methods must match the speed of the targets of interest while
expanding the accessible imaging area.
Most current methods primarily focus on expanding the area imaged at typical calcium framerates (30 Hz
or slower) through multi-plane and volumetric imaging approaches. Methods to improve speed have also
been explored, in particular focusing on pre-selection of regions-of-interest (ROIs), which minimize the
time spent imaging areas with little signal. These approaches can improve imaging speed but require
pre-selection of ROIs, limiting the ability to freely explore tissue and missing ROIs not presenting strong
signals in the short initialization scan, and can be sensitive to motion artifacts---especially those that
move the ROI partly or fully out of the imaged area targeting the ROI. As an alternative, we propose a
computational imaging technique that combines the speed gains from sub-sampling each frame with the
benefit of reconstructing the full FOV.
Our approach combines the blurring local information in only one dimension of the scan (i.e., the
direction of slowest scanning) and randomly selecting only a fraction of lines for each frame, which are
fully sampled. We further leverage the well-used low-rank model of spatio-temporal correlations in
fluorescence videos to fill in the missing regions through a matrix completion reconstruction. Our
preliminary data shows feasibility of the reconstruction in both two-photon and light-sheet settings,
meaning that our conceptual approach is broadly applicable to a range of imaging technologies. Through
minimal modifications and development and optimization of the reconstruction algorithm we propose to
build and validate 1) a two-photon microscope capable of imaging a 0.5 micon FOV at >400 Hz (Aim 1)
and 2) a light-sheet microscope capable of full-brain zebrafish imaging at >200 Hz (Aim 2). We will
demonstrate these technologies in densely labeled glutamate imaging in mice (Aim 1), and in full-brain
voltage imaging in zebrafish (Aim 2).

title: Slippery Omniphobic Coating for Hemodialysis Catheter to Resist Fibrin Sheathing and Infection and Improve Patient Outcomes
text:
Many patients undergoing hemodialysis require use of a catheter to secure vascular access, but complication
rates are high due to infections and thrombosis; however, no available solutions successfully prevent both
these complications. We developed a coating technology to reduce the complication rate with catheter use
during hemodialysis by ameliorating thrombosis and infections, and our previous work optimized the coating
procedure for hemodialysis catheters. In this proposal, we will complete our path to marketability with the long-
term goal of improving the outcomes of patient requiring hemodialysis by reducing infection and thrombosis-
related complications.

title: Genetically Engineered Mouse Models (GEMM)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MOUSE MODELS SHARED RESOURCE The Genetically Engineered Mouse Models Shared Resource (GEMMSR), formerly the Transgenic Gene Knockout Shared Resource, provides St. Jude Comprehensive Cancer Center (SJCCC) members with convenient and economic access to generating genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs). This includes the production of transgenic, knock-out, conditional knock-out, deletion, and knock-in mouse lines. These models are critical tools for advancing science at the SJCCC by elucidating the role of genetic changes in the initiation and progression of cancer and deciphering the mechanisms through which therapeutic targets operate in anticancer treatment. The GEMMSR is directed by Youngwook Ahn, PhD, who has over 18 years of transgenic and GEMM creation experience and is supported by three full-time, highly experienced staff members. The GEMMSR provides a range of services, including consultation, classic transgenics, CRISPR editing via pronuclear injection, CRISPR editing via electroporation, and extended genotyping. The CRISPR editing with electroporation of zygotes and extended genotyping services were newly introduced during the project period. With this additional method for creating mouse lines, the GEMMSR increased the live birth rates of all GEMMs from ~6% to ~25% and reduced the number of zygotes required. During the project period, several additional changes were made. The GEMMSR retired the mouse embryonic stem cell arm of the facility due to decreased demand, allowing for a greater focus on CRISPR-based animal model creation. Additionally, the GEMMSR decided to stop maintaining an in-house C57BL/6 donor colony, opting instead to purchase these mice from an external vendor. This change reduced the overall number of animals and cages maintained and contributed to an increase in live birth rates. Due to these changes and increases in efficiency, GEMMSR staffing was reduced by two staff members, while at the same time nearly doubling GEMMSR capacity. During the project period, the GEMMSR moved to the newly constructed Vivarium and i4 Advanced Research Center, increasing the GEMMSR to a total of 2,119 sq ft. During the reference year (FY2024), the GEMMSR provided services to 17 investigators at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. Among these investigators, 14 (82%) were SJCCC members from four of the five research Programs. Additionally, 93% of the chargebacks were attributed to SJCCC members. Key services completed in FY2024 include producing five transgenic lines and completing 38 CRISPR/Cas9-targeting projects. These projects comprised 14 conditional knockouts, one knockout, one deletion, and 22 knock-in mouse lines. Additionally, GEMMSR staff are involved in education and training on GEMMSR technologies and services through a variety of platforms including the SR Expo, lab tours, and lectures to graduate students. The GEMMSR has been highly impactful during the current project period, as evidenced by 49 publications from SJCCC members reporting usage of GEMMSR services with 29 (59%) being in high- impact journals (impact factor >10).

title: INROADS Project 2
text: SUMMARY – Project 2: Signatures and Classifiers of Peanut Desensitization (SPADE) Peanut allergy is a clinical and public health problem that affects 2.2% of children and 1.8% of adults in the United States. While there remains no cure for peanut allergy, desensitization treatment reduces sensitivity to peanut such that small exposures may not lead to reaction, reducing risk of severe allergic reactions and providing reassurance to peanut allergic individuals. Desensitization can be achieved by: (1) immunotherapy, commonly oral immunotherapy (OIT), where peanut protein is introduced and incorporated via gradually increasing daily ingestion, and (2) omalizumab, an anti-IgE biologic medication recently approved by the FDA for food allergy treatment. Both OIT and omalizumab allow peanut allergic individuals to achieve desensitization, but their detailed mechanisms have yet to be fully discerned and compared. There are no biomarkers to predict who will succeed with treatment and no biomarkers to determine that desensitization has been achieved. During our last AADCRC, we transcriptomically profiled children with high-threshold peanut allergy and identified a peripheral blood signature and classifier of OIT-induced desensitization. The central goal of this AADCRC’s Project 2, Signatures and Classifiers of Peanut Desensitization (SPADE) is to deepen mechanistic understanding of the treatment modalities currently available for peanut allergic individuals, and to develop and test classifiers for their clinical implementation to improve the management of peanut allergic individuals. We will study peanut allergic children undergoing oral food challenges before and after 1 year of omalizumab or peanut OIT. Children of all reaction thresholds will be included. We hypothesize that: peanut desensitization achieved with omalizumab will demonstrate a significantly different peripheral blood transcriptional signature compared to desensitization achieved by peanut OIT (Aim 1); peanut allergy desensitization achieved with omalizumab can be accurately classified by selected peripheral blood transcripts identified by machine learning (Aim 2); and the classifier of peanut OIT-induced desensitization that we identified during our last AADCRC in children with high-threshold peanut allergy will perform well in peanut allergic children of any reaction threshold undergoing real-world OIT (Aim 3). We will leverage a well-characterized clinical cohort from our AADCRC’s Clinical Core, RNA sequencing (bulk and single cell), rigorous statistical models, and machine learning to address our hypotheses. The deliverables from SPADE will include: (1) identification of a peripheral blood transcriptional signature of omalizumab- induced peanut desensitization and its comparative analysis to signatures of peanut OIT-induced desensitization; (2) machine learning-driven discovery of a peripheral blood classifier of omalizumab-induced peanut desensitization; and (3) performance testing of a peripheral blood-based classifier of peanut OIT- induced desensitization in children with peanut allergy of widely ranging reaction thresholds. This project will deepen understanding of desensitization mechanisms and provide clinical tools for treating peanut allergy. .

title: Core B - Large Animal Core
text:
(Core B)
Large Animal Model and Electrophysiology Core
All three Projects in this P01 include experiments in neonatal and adult pigs, which are typically too complex and
expensive to be conducted in an individual lab. Thus, by providing a centralized facility for all surgical procedures,
functional assessments and electrophysiological evaluations, the Large Animal Core (Core B) will maximize data
quality and experimental efficiency while minimizing the costs associated with these studies.

title: Longitudinal Analysis of Immune Signatures (IMS) of M. tuberculosis-specific T cells
text: Project 2 Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) and is a leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide. Here we will characterize immune signatures (IMS) of Mtb antigen-specific CD4 T cells in individuals with different states of Mtb infection and BCG vaccination. Specifically, we will utilize our established Mtb peptide epitope pools and assay systems to identify antigen- specific CD4 T cells and their T cell receptors (TCRs). The IMS will be further characterized in cytometry and single-cell RNA-seq assays after antigen stimulation and ex vivo. For Aim 1, we will enroll cohorts of individuals with active tuberculosis (ATB), characterized by uncontrolled symptomatic Mtb infection, who will be receiving anti-TB therapy. We will longitudinally track the IMS over the course of treatment, and identify markers predictive of treatment outcomes. For Aim 2, we will enroll individuals with ‘latent’ TB infection (LTBI), which is characterized by immune reactivity to Mtb but no symptoms of disease (i.e. Mtb reactive). LTBI is heterogeneous, consisting both of individuals who have successfully cleared their infection and display a memory immune response, as well as others with subclinical infection at increased risk of developing active disease. There is currently no test available to distinguish subclinical from cleared infection. We will determine the IMS in prophylactically-treated LTBI longitudinally, and determine who displays a treatment response most similar to ATB, which we consider most likely to have had subclinical disease. For a separate cohort of LTBI, we will utilize a unique human challenge model to obtain samples with antigen-specific resident T cells from the lung and use them to evaluate overlap and differences between the IMS in the blood vs. lung from the same set of individuals. For Aim 3, we will obtain samples taken pre- and post-BCG (re)vaccination in adults to characterize the vaccine induced IMS. Revaccination of Mtb uninfected adults has been shown to be protective from disease, thus, comparing this IMS with that in LTBI (controlled infection) vs. ATB (uncontrolled infection) can reveal protective components of vaccine induced immunity.

title: Biostatistic and Patient Registry Core
text:
The Biostatistics, Bioinformatics and Patient Registry Core is comprised of individuals with expertise in
biostatistics and/or bioinformatics as well as understanding of factors that impact the development and growth
of breast cancer. Their efforts in developing study designs and analysis plans to evaluate the research
hypotheses ensures the issue of confounding factors is addressed, reliable and reproducible measurement
techniques are employed, emerging scientific insights are incorporated into ongoing studies, and a sufficient
number of patients/specimens/mice are utilized to draw conclusions. The care in which studies are designed,
conducted, analyzed, and interpreted will impact whether the results are seen as providing insights that should
be acted on and further built upon or not.

title: Identifying and characterizing molecular and circuitry-based heterogeneity of AgRP neurons.
text:
Obesity is among the most pressing and costly medical challenges confronting modern society. While neurons
that express agouti-related protein (AgRP) are implicated in the regulation of energy balance, our recent work
suggests there are distinct subsets of AgRP neurons that mediate different metabolic and behavioral functions.
The identification and characterization of distinct subsets of AgRP neurons, and mapping their downstream
projections will advance our understanding of energy homeostasis and has the potential to identify novel
therapeutic strategies for obesity.

title: Core B
text: CORE B: ABSTRACT Core B (Clinical and Imaging Core) will support Projects 1-3 for new clinical and translational research in schizophrenia (SZ) and relevant animal models. Core B is built on our established cohesive and committed team of investigators, with experts in clinical enrollment and characterization, olfactory imaging, and cortical imaging [as a productive outcome of long-term collaboration between the Johns Hopkins Schizophrenia Center (JHSZC) and the Center for Imaging Science (CIS) at Johns Hopkins University]. Smell deficits are one of the most reproducible changes in SZ. One key feature of the deficits is their tight association with specific clinical features, such as negative symptoms (e.g., avolition, anhedonia) and some cognitive deficits (e.g., social cognitive deficits), but not with positive symptoms (e.g., hallucination, delusion). Since 2009, the NIMH Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework has facilitated studies that focus on neurobiological processes underlying behavioral domains/constructs, instead of considering each psychiatric diagnosis as one homogeneous entity. One innovation of this P50 is translational research with both human and mouse studies under specific behavioral domains/constructs of interest (mainly, positive valence systems and social processes) in a mechanistic association with the olfactory-prefrontal circuits to account for specific clinical domains in SZ. Thus, we will leverage the RDoC research framework to organize our research design. Based on this framework, this Core B will assist Projects in addressing the central hypothesis that, mediated by the olfactory-prefrontal circuits, molecular and cellular changes in the olfactory epithelium (OE) significantly contribute to specific clinical manifestations that correlate with smell deficits in SZ patients. Accordingly, Core B will recruit new study participants and conduct clinical assessments, combining with the existing cohort (Aim 1). We will leverage a recently established alliance of patient recruitment with the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center (MPRC) and 10 hospitals in the MedStar Health network. We will pay a special attention to the confounding factors associated with COVID-19 in study participant recruitment and data analysis in collaboration with Core C (Core for data analysis). Core B will also collect and process brain imaging data (Aim 2) to provide ex vivo mouse olfactory bulb (OB) imaging (for Project 1), process 3T resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from human healthy subjects (for Project 2), and obtain 3T structural imaging of the OB and prefrontal cortex from newly recruited subjects in this grant proposal (for Project 3). In summary, this Core B will acquire multimodal data from both humans and mice under a specific scientific focus on the olfactory-prefrontal circuits.

title: Natural Products for Microbiome-Targeted Therapies
text:
This research will establish cyclic oligosaccharides (COs) as a novel class of natural products for precision
microbiome engineering by leveraging their unique ability to create exclusive metabolic niches accessible only
to bacteria with specialized metabolic machinery. We will develop CO-based strategies for both targeted
enhancement of beneficial native microbes through precision prebiotics and reliable engraftment of engineered
therapeutic strains through synthetic exclusive metabolic niches, enabling unprecedented control over
microbial community composition and function. Through computational discovery and experimental validation,
this work will expand the toolkit of available CO systems and establish a versatile platform for multi-species
microbiome manipulation with applications in both therapeutic interventions and experimental research models.

title: Sleep-specific DBS therapy in Parkinson's disease
text:
Sleep-wake disturbances are a major factor associated with reduced quality of life of individuals with
Parkinson's disease (PD), a progressive neurological disorder affecting millions of people in the U.S and
worldwide. The brain mechanisms underlying these sleep disorders, and the effects of therapeutic interventions
such as deep brain stimulation on sleep-related neuronal activity and sleep behavior, are not well understood.
Results from this study will provide a better understanding of the brain circuitry involved in disordered sleep in
PD and inform the development of targeted therapeutic interventions to treat sleep disorders in people with
neurodegenerative disease.

title: Energy Metabolism Reprograming in Smooth Muscle Cell in Aortic Disease Progression
text: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (ATAAD) are life-threatening conditions with no effective medical therapies to halt aneurysm progression or prevent dissection. Smooth muscle cells (SMCs), the principal cell type maintaining aortic wall integrity, undergo a phenotypic switch during disease progression: an adaptive, extracellular matrix (ECM)-producing response predominates in aneurysm (ATAA), while a maladaptive inflammatory response characterizes dissection (ATAD). The molecular driver controlling this transition remains unknown, representing a critical barrier to developing therapies that stabilize aneurysms and prevent catastrophic rupture. Preliminary single-cell RNA-seq and integrative GWAS/eQTL analyses from the applicant's laboratory reveal that ATAA and ATAD are marked by distinct patterns of energy metabolism reprogramming in SMCs. ATAA is characterized by elevated mitochondrial gene expression with modest glycolytic and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) changes, whereas ATAD shows a pronounced shift toward glycolysis accompanied by suppressed FAO and mitochondrial gene expression. These findings, together with identification of PRDM6 as a candidate causal gene at an aortic disease GWAS locus, led to the central hypothesis that PRDM6 drives energy metabolism reprogramming that dictates SMC phenotypic trajectory, which regulates aortic disease progression. This hypothesis will be tested through two specific aims. Aim 1 will determine the functional role of energy metabolism in directing SMC phenotype and aortic disease progression, using pharmacologic and genetic blockade of glycolysis (galactose) or FAO (etomoxir/Cpt1a knockout) in human SMCs and in a SMC-specific Cpt1a deficient ATAAD mouse model. Aim 2 will test PRDM6 as a molecular driver of this metabolic reprogramming, using PRDM6 knockdown in human SMCs, and will query PRDM6's in vivo regulatory role using a SMC specific Prdm6 deficient mouse model subjected to ATAAD induction. Completion of this project will define a novel metabolic and epigenetic mechanism governing the adaptiveto- inflammatory SMC phenotypic switch in aortic disease, establishing the conceptual and experimental foundation for metabolism-targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at stabilizing aneurysms and preventing dissection.

title: Contributions of the Wnt Signaling Pathway on cell and tissue morphometrics during early limb blastma formation
text:
The axolotl salamander can fully regenerate various complex structures, including whole
limbs. This project will investigate the contributions of the Wnt signaling pathway on cell
and tissue morphometrics on formation of an early limb blastema. This project is essential
for understanding the Wnt regulated cell and tissue dynamics during limb regeneration in
the axolotl, which may allow for novel therapeutic targets for tissue and limb regeneration
in humans.

title: Exposing versus Hiding: A Novel Nanoplatform for Nasal Universal Flu Vaccines
text:
Influenza is the leading cause of hospitalizations and death by respiratory infection. We will engineer a new plug-
and-play EV platform and conjugate inverted HA onto the surface of the EVs as intranasal influenza vaccines to
achieve broad protective influenza immunity in both systemic compartments and local sites against influenza A
and B. The implementation and success of the project will improve public health by conferring broad cross-
protection against influenza epidemics and occasional pandemics.
